transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-07
Start time (PDT): 15:00
Duration: ~1h18m
Attendees: Priya Patel (Redwood AE), Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE), Hannah Lee (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (Sierra Lead), Lauren Kim (SRE), Evan Sato (CTO), Maya Ortiz (SRE)

Summary:
Quick hands-on workshop to align on an apples-vs-apples (standardized baseline) approach for latency/throughput benchmarking: prompt set curation, load generation protocols, KV/prefix cache toggles, batching behavior, and quantization effects. Discussed VPC/on-prem constraints for network-limited workloads and agreed on next-steps for an instrumented bench run on Redwood Dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Prompt set selection & token-length distribution
- Load generation tooling and ramp patterns (open-loop vs closed-loop)
- Defining fairness: model variants, sequence length, sampling parameters
- KV cache and prefix caching effects on tail latency
- Batching strategies: max batch size, latency SLOs, dynamic batching windows
- Quantization tradeoffs and regression checks
- VPC/on-prem constraints, egress, and peering for bench runs

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, auto-transcribed — some words may be off):
[00:00] Priya: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run for about an hour, the goal here is, um, to lock down a repeatable methodology so both teams can reproduce latencies and cost numbers. sound good?
[00:09] Rajiv: yeah sounds great. i want to be very clear on what counts as fair, like if you run with q4 but we run q5 that's not apples — so i'd like a checklist.
[00:17] Mateo: totally, and we'll define the matrix: quantization, KV cache on/off, batching policy, and route (hosted/dedicated/private). we'll produce a runbook.
[00:28] Lauren: quick network note — our private racks have a 25Gbps egress and strict firewall so if we're doing peering we need details on subnets and ip ranges, vpn, etc.
[00:37] Hannah: noted, we'll attach our VPC peering doc, plus an on-prem runner option if peering is not allowed.
[00:44] Evan: also curious about what load tool you recommend — we use locust for HTTP but it's not token-aware.
[00:50] Mateo: yeah so good question. for token-aware load we usually use a custom harness (we call it redwood-harness) that replays prompt lengths and simulates streaming. we can also provide a locust plugin. the key is open-loop vs closed-loop behavior.
[01:03] Rajiv: can you explain the difference for our use case?
[01:06] Mateo: sure — open-loop fires requests at a fixed RPS regardless of latency, so you measure throughput saturation, tail latencies will blow up once queueing happens. closed-loop keeps concurrency bounded by waiting on responses, so it's more representative of client-side latency SLOs. for LLM inference both are useful: open-loop to measure max throughput/efficiency, closed-loop for p95/p99 user impact.
[01:30] Priya: and we should record p50/p95/p99 and also tokens/sec and cost-per-1k-tokens.
[01:37] Rajiv: agreed. also we need to test with sequence-length distributions that reflect our catalog queries — mostly short (<=64) but 5-10% are longer (512+).
[01:46] Hannah: can you share token distribution?
[01:48] Rajiv: i'll upload a histogram csv.
[01:51] Mateo: perfect. on KV cache — quick primer: prefix/KV cache keeps key-value layers per session so repeated prefixes are served from memory and avoid recomputing attention past keys. in practice, for chatty flows with repeated system prompts, the cache can reduce per-token latency by ~20-60% depending on hit rate.
[02:13] Lauren: how do you simulate cold vs warm cache? that's critical.
[02:17] Mateo: two ways: one, seed the harness with warm sessions (warm-up phase), or two, run cold sessions by rotating conversation ids so no cache hits occur. we recommend both and report both sets.
[02:28] Rajiv: ok include both. also what about KV size limits? our old infra blew up when cache on GPU exceeded mem for 1K convs.
[02:36] Mateo: good point. we'll provide a mem profile per config (model, quantization) and a per-GPU KV capacity estimate. it's an output in the runbook.
[02:44] Evan: quantization — what profiles do you recommend? int8, q4, q5b? we need to watch quality regressions.
[02:50] Hannah: we typically test q4_0, q5_1, and int8 (where supported). also include fp16 baseline. and tie quality checks to a prompt set with reference answers and automatic NLI/regression thresholds.
[03:03] Priya: yes — for "apples-vs-apples" we lock random seeds, sampling (temperature, top_p) and use deterministic decoding (greedy or sampling with fixed seed) for perf runs. quality runs are separate.
[03:16] Rajiv: about batching — we saw during our internal tests that batching helps throughput but increases tail a lot. how do you configure dynamic batching windows?
[03:24] Mateo: we tune the batching window (latency budget) — e.g., keep max batch wait at 5ms for low-latency SLOs, up to 50ms for cost-optimized throughput. Redwood's runtime also supports continuous batching so that KV-cache hits can bypass some recompute. we can expose these knobs in the harness.
[03:44] Lauren: example numbers?
[03:46] Mateo: rough numbers: short-seq workloads (<=64) with batch=8 and q4 might get you 3–6x throughput improvement vs batch=1. tail p99 could move from 120ms to 220ms depending on batching window and queueing. numbers depend a lot on GPU type and sequence mix.
[04:05] Evan: GPU type — are we testing on A10 vs A100 or H100? we have preference for A10 in prod.
[04:10] Priya: for a fair matrix we suggest: A10 (cost-optimized), A100 (balanced), and H100 (peak). Redwood Dedicated can provision A10 and A100; H100 is limited. we'll note hardware explicitly in the benchmark table.
[04:26] Rajiv: we need network egress effects captured — some models exceed 5ms per-token because of cross-region lookups to our customer DB. can we simulate network add-on latency?
[04:36] Mateo: yes harness can add synthetic network delays and payload size variation. but try to isolate inference-only latency first; then run integrated tests with network stubs.
[04:46] Maya: for VPC/on-prem runs, how do we collect traces? we need token-level tracing to map spikes to KV misses or batching delays.
[04:54] Hannah: we can ship a lightweight tracer that logs request meta (batch size, seq length, kv_hit boolean, kernel selection, latency_ms). it won't contain prompt text unless you opt-in for debug. logs are linkable to trace IDs in Redwood Console.
[05:10] Rajiv: one more — what about warm-started KV across sessions (sticky routing)? our app pins sessions to a user to keep cache locality.
[05:18] Mateo: we can simulate sticky routing by using a hash key per user ID in harness; we'll include that as a mode. good to test both sticky and random routing.
[05:27] Evan: how will you compare models? we have several open models we want to test plus a Redwood-verified variant.
[05:33] Priya: the runbook will define: exact model commit (hash), tokenizer version, quantization artifact, and a canonical prompt set. we also normalize for sampling params. every run will log model string so we can reproduce.
[05:44] Rajiv: i want an example bench matrix, something like:
- model vX baseline fp16 A100 batch policies (1,8,16) KV on/off
- model vX q4 A10 batch (1,8) KV on/off
- model vY q5 H100 ...
[05:58] Hannah: yep we'll output a csv of configs and a dashboard with p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost-per-1m-tokens.
[06:07] Priya: on quality/rightness checks we recommend three tiers: smoke perf, functional equivalence (automated similarity thresholds using rouge/bleu/qa exact match), and human spot checks for edge cases.
[06:19] Rajiv: acceptable. do you have a standard prompt-set template?
[06:22] Mateo: yes, we'll share a "prompt-suite" with categories: short-instruction, long-context, multi-turn, retrieval-augmented prompt, and noisy inputs. each prompt has expected token distribution and a golden answer for quals.
[06:35] Lauren: items about cost math — what's included in cost-per-token? GPU time only or infra (network, storage)?
[06:41] Priya: we break down unit economics: GPU GPU-minutes, NVME I/O where relevant, networking egress, and orchestration overhead. the Console will attribute token-level cost.
[06:51] Rajiv: can we replicate with our on-prem infra? we have a cage with 4x A10s, but no shared filesystem.
[06:58] Hannah: runner supports local mode: it ships a small docker that executes same harness. it sends metrics to a provided metrics endpoint over TLS. we'll provide run instructions in the repo.
[07:07] Evan: about safety/compliance — in on-prem runs do you require sending any request content upstream?
[07:12] Priya: no — on-prem mode can operate fully air-gapped. the only thing we'd ask for is metrics reporting endpoint or offline artifact uploads. we also have an option to encrypt artifacts with your KMS.
[07:24] Rajiv: good. one concern — caching can be nondeterministic across model implementations. how do we handle that when normalizing?
[07:31] Mateo: we propose to report uncached (cold) and cached (warm) separately, and also provide per-run seed and detailed logs. if runtime kernel selection differs, that's a runtime difference and must be part of the documentation. the idea is transparency not forced identical internal implementations.
[07:51] Lauren: for the bench UI — can we see batch-size distribution over time?
[07:56] Hannah: yes we'll expose histograms: batch size, seq length, kv hit rate, and latency per bucket.
[08:03] Rajiv: ok from the customer's side timeline — we want initial synthetic bench within two weeks, then one integrated test with our app flows in three weeks.
[08:11] Priya: sounds reasonable. we'll provision a Dedicated test cluster and schedule the bench run the week of 2025-10-20.
[08:19] Evan: any risks or gotchas?
[08:21] Mateo: network throttling, misconfigured token limits, and mismatch in tokenizer versions are common gotchas. also quant artifacts can change memory and kernel paths, so watch OOMs.
[08:33] Rajiv: noted. please add a preflight checklist.
[08:36] Hannah: we'll add: tokenizer check, model commit hash, quant artifact checksum, GPU driver version, and network sanity test.
[08:46] Priya: ok last bit — can you share an initial bench plan right after the call? we'll include exact commands.
[08:52] Mateo: yes, repo link and runbook will be in the next steps.
[09:00] Lauren: thanks all — this was super helpful.

Meeting wrap / quick recap:
[09:06] Priya: recap: repo + runbook shared, customer uploads canonical prompts + token histogram, Redwood will provision Dedicated cluster window and propose quant profiles. both teams to agree on final bench matrix by 2025-10-17. next call to review results after initial synthetic runs.
